Introducing
AT1.

15.2 kg of thrust from four powerful motors on 8.5-inch tri-blade props and a one-piece PAHT frame. A compact quad that lifts like a much bigger one and takes serious crashes, built for training and for fun.

Made for flying

Small frame.
Heavy lift.
Built to crash.

AT1, Airolit Training 1, isn't a work drone. It's a compact 332 mm quad that lifts over 7 kg, for pilots who want to learn how a heavy-lift drone handles without the size of one, and for anyone who wants to fly something with serious punch. The one-piece frame is built to withstand serious crashes, so training mistakes don't end the session.

01
Training

Learn heavy lift

Practise flying with real payloads, and get used to how weight changes braking, inertia and wind handling, on a frame small enough to carry anywhere.

  • Plenty of thrust in reserve for recovering mistakes
  • One-piece PAHT frame built to take serious crashes
  • 20×20 flight controller and 55 A ESC included, with XT60 power
02
Fun

Power to play with

15 kilos of thrust on a 544 g quad is a lot. Punch-outs, long cruises and big smooth lines are what it's for.

  • 8.5-inch tri-blade props for grip and fast response
  • Room on board for a camera if you want footage
  • Rail system underneath for batteries and payloads

Flight time

Battery, payload,
flight time.

AT1 runs on a high-power 6S pack. With a 22 Ah high-density pack it flies for over an hour with nothing on board in ideal conditions. Bigger packs fly longer but weigh more, and so does anything you carry. Move the sliders to see the trade-off.

Battery type

Calculated from bench-test data for the motors on 8.5-inch tri-blades: ideal conditions, cruising at around 10 m/s in still air at sea level, which is about 10% more efficient than hovering. Li-ion and high-density packs are flown down to 3.0 V per cell (empty is 2.6 V), which uses about 95% of the pack; LiPo uses 80%. Assumes about 325 Wh/kg for high-density, 230 Wh/kg for Li-ion and 145 Wh/kg for LiPo. Hovering, wind and hard flying use more power, so expect less in everyday flying.

The frame

One piece.
No loose plates.

Most heavy-lift quads are a stack of flat plates and standoffs. AT1 is a single body in high-strength PAHT, with curved bracing between every arm, so the load from full throttle spreads through the whole frame instead of into a few bolted joints. The same structure soaks up impacts, so it withstands serious crashes.

    Underside

    Rail system.

    Twin rails run along the underside of the frame. Batteries and payloads mount to them, so the same airframe can carry anything from a 5 Ah pack to a 36 Ah pack, or a camera or sensor.

    Batteries

    Any pack size

    Small packs for light, punchy flying and big packs for long sessions all fit the same rails.

    Payloads

    Carry what you need

    Cameras, sensors or test weights mount underneath, keeping the top of the frame clear.

    Power

    Straight to the XT60

    The battery lead plugs into the XT60 housing at the back of the frame.
